inline.s: For those who dare to climb and shrink from no hardship, Buddha-recitation in the breath has a most solid path: first practice according to
Practical Insight Meditation

to cultivate the power of awareness by making the rising and falling of the abdomen the core of your attention. When the skill of awareness has matured, then on that foundation recite the Buddha’s name with awareness, following the rising and falling of the abdomen, in a continuous, close-packed stream; this is naturally the state of one mind undisturbed. (Please note: this borrows the basic exercises of insight meditation in order to train and cultivate a focused, continuous, and enduring power of awareness, laying the foundation for Buddha-recitation in the breath. So in using the insight meditation books, the key is to read the basic exercises.)
Q: I say one “Amitābha Buddha” on the in-breath and one “Amitābha Buddha” on the out-breath. Is that all right?
A: Yes. Reciting the Buddha in the breath this way is also very effective.
Master Yinguang says:
“Guang
(the Master’s own way of referring to himself)
has believed in the one Dharma of the Pure Land ever since leaving home. But because
(but since)

obstructed by karmic obstacles, for twenty years I drifted and idly passed the time. Though the mouth recited the Buddha, the mind took no dye from the Way. Recently, urged on by a Dharma master’s encouragement, I vowed not to fail his grandmotherly heart. But drowsiness and scatteredness attack by turns, and I go on as before. So day by day I read more than ten pages of Pure Land texts to rouse a mind of surpassing progress. As for the jewel-king method of following the breath, I tried it, and at once felt that deluded thoughts no longer surged and churned as before. I think that in time there must come a day when the fog scatters, the clouds melt, and the sky and sun are seen clear through. ... Guang also holds that this one method contains all five contemplations that stop the mind. If one recites the Buddha following the breath, that includes both the contemplation of counting the breath and the contemplation of the Buddha
(that is, it includes the contemplation of counting the breath and the contemplation of the Buddha: counting the breath stops scatteredness, the contemplation of the Buddha stops karmic obstacles)
, and it is again the method by which Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva
(this is again the method of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva: ‘gathering in the six sense faculties, pure thoughts in succession’)
, gathers in the six sense faculties
. And by gathering in the mind to recite the Buddha, the tainted mind can gradually be cut off
(stopping greed)
, anger will surely not blaze
(stopping anger)
, and once drowsiness and scatteredness are gone, wisdom appears before one, so delusion too can be broken
(stopping delusion)

. I hold that those who nowadays recite the Buddha in a careless, slipshod way should probably not be told to rely on this method; I fear that, because they do not keep count, they will only grow lazy. But one who has the will, if he does not rely on this method, will certainly find it hard to attain samādhi. The Dharma master, riding his vow to benefit others, need not use it himself, but he should try it out for the sake of later students, to teach those who come after. One of keen faculties will surely attain one mind within one seven-day period, or two. As for one as dull and inferior as Guang, I think that in ten or eight years he may perhaps be undisturbed.”
(Letter to Master Dixian)

[The five contemplations that stop the mind] Contemplations that can stop five faults (greed, anger, delusion, karmic obstacles, and scatteredness) from arising in the mind. One: the contemplation of impurity — observing that all bodies and all worlds are impure, in order to stop greed. Two: the contemplation of compassion — observing the pitiable suffering of all sentient beings, in order to stop anger. Three: the contemplation of causes and conditions — observing that all dharmas arise from causes and conditions, cause and effect following one upon the other in perfect clarity, in order to stop delusion. Four: the contemplation of the Buddha — observing the Buddha’s physical marks and the splendor of his virtues, in order to stop karmic obstacles. Five: the contemplation of counting the breath — observing the arising and passing of the breath, counting each in-breath and out-breath silently from one to ten, in order to stop scatteredness. [The method by which Mahāsthāmaprāpta gathers in the six sense faculties] The “Chapter on Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva” says:

“The Buddha asked about perfect penetration. I had no choice to make: I gathered in all six sense faculties, and my pure thoughts continued without interruption, and so I attained samādhi. This is the foremost method.”

(Translation: When the Buddha asked how perfect penetration is attained, I did not choose any other method, but simply gathered in the six sense faculties, so that deluded thoughts no longer arose, and only the thought of remembering the Buddha continued unbroken; and so I attained Buddha-recitation samādhi. This way of practice is the most excellent of all.) [The six sense faculties] Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. [Pure thoughts in succession] The thought of remembering the Buddha without interval. [Samādhi] That is, sanmei.

If Buddha-recitation in the breath is joined with qigong, it can also drive out illness and lengthen life — as it is said, when the body is at peace the Way flourishes. The method is this: sitting, lying, or standing are all acceptable; touch the tongue to the upper palate, breathe in and out through the nose, and when you breathe in, fill yourself completely; when you breathe out, empty yourself completely (if you cannot do this at first, then slow down and work up to it step by step). As you breathe in, recite “Amitābha Buddha”, let the abdomen swell outward, and bring the qi down to the dantian; then as you breathe out, recite “Amitābha Buddha”, and let the abdomen draw inward. The breathing should be soft and effortless. Throughout the recitation, always be aware of the dantian (holding the mind on the dantian), and gradually bring it about that the mind is free of random thoughts: this is the key to cultivating both nature and life.

[Dantian] Here it means the lower dantian, which is the Guanyuan point on the Conception Vessel, three inches (four fingers’ width) below the navel; it is the place where essence is stored. The lower dantian is the main site for training, gathering, and storing true qi. A person’s primal qi originates in the kidneys and is stored in the dantian; by way of the triple burner it circulates through the whole body, driving the functional activity of the five viscera and six bowels. A person’s strength or weakness, life and death, all depend on whether the primal qi of the dantian is full or depleted; therefore it is very important to care for the primal qi of the dantian. When the primal qi of the dantian is full and abundant, one can mobilize the body’s latent powers, so that true qi circulates through the whole body. Holding the mind on the dantian can regulate yin and yang, open communication between heart and kidneys, fill and free the true qi through the eight vessels, restore the innate physiological functions, and promote health and long life.
The Forty-Eight Methods of Buddha-Recitation by Name
says:

“Or again, when the breath is calm and the mind at peace, first visualize your own body as standing within a circle of light; silently observe the tip of the nose and attend to the in-breath and out-breath. With each breath
(the out-breath and the in-breath each count as one breath)
silently say the name of Amitābha Buddha once, adjusting the breath with skill, neither slow nor hurried, mind and breath leaning on each other, following the breath as it goes out and comes in.
Walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, it can be practiced at all times; do not let it be interrupted, but constantly hold it in secret.

When the mind has been gathered in for a long time, breath and thought are both forgotten, and this very body and mind become equal to empty space. Recite until utterly proficient, and the eye of the mind opens; samādhi suddenly appears before you — and this is the Pure Land of the mind-only!”
Q: Can one recite the Buddha in the breath while walking?

A: Yes. The method is this: while walking, silently recite “Amitābha Buddha”, one word to a step; four steps to one in-breath, four steps to one out-breath. This method is wonderful, but like riding a bicycle, it has to be learned; once mastered, its benefits are boundless. The breathing is still abdominal: the abdomen swells outward on the in-breath and draws inward on the out-breath.
Q: I cannot sustain Buddha-recitation in the breath for long; after a while I feel tightness in the chest and shortness of breath, and it is very uncomfortable. What should I do?
A: The essential point of Buddha-recitation in the breath is this:
following the breath

. That is, recite the Buddha following the natural breath, and do not try to control or change the breathing. The breath during Buddha-recitation in the breath should be the same as when you are not reciting. What you need to do now is to carefully experience how to recite following the breath (working on the word “following”) without controlling or changing the breathing. First train in a still state; only when the skill is proficient in stillness should you gradually do it in movement.

Q: After reciting the Buddha in the breath for a long time, I sometimes feel the breath is not smooth. Later I used swelling and drawing in the abdomen to help the abdominal breathing: I breathe in as the abdomen swells, and breathe out as it draws in. That solved the problem of the breath not being smooth. May I recite the Buddha in the breath this way?
A: Certainly.

Q: When I recite sitting down, I lightly tap with my finger, one tap to a word, five phrases to a set, aware of every word; each time I finish a set, I check whether any delusion has arisen, and then rouse my awareness and recite the next set; and so on over and over. Reciting the Buddha this way, I have very few deluded thoughts, and even if one arises I can spot it at once and put it out at once. May I do it this way?

A: Yes. The Dharma has no fixed method; the wonder of its use lies in the one mind. So long as it accords with the principle of “perfect clarity, neither dull nor scattered, enduring and resistant to distraction,” it is good. You may also prepare several ways of reciting, to suit different situations. But a reminder: this method has two crutches — tapping with the finger and checking every five phrases. These are expedients for the beginning; when your skill runs deep, do not lean on them any longer. Of course, when difficulties come, you may pick up the crutches at any time and get through the hard passage.

Buddha-recitation must start from real combat. When you meet a situation and encounter a condition, to be able not to forget the Buddha’s name is one great victory. When a deluded thought arises, to be able at once to turn it away with the Buddha’s name is another great victory. You must often and deliberately polish yourself against situations and conditions, winning these two victories again and again; then the highest grade may be hoped for.
Q: Why does the text so often speak of cultivation, refining, and skill?

A: To cultivate is to repair and set right, to restore to perfection. To refine is to smelt: the mind-nature of sentient beings is like gold in ore — smelt away the dross and pure gold is obtained. It also means to forge: the mind-nature of sentient beings is like stubborn iron — hammered again and again, a hundred forgings make it steel. As for the word “skill,” it means the time and energy spent in practice, and also the level of attainment reached by that practice. Master Yinguang states plainly: cultivation-virtue “is what skill brings about.”

[A hundred forgings make steel] The ancient craft of smelting iron into steel. An iron block, heated red and then hammered, has its structure refined, becomes denser, its composition more even, and its impurities driven out, until it becomes steel of very great hardness and yet tough. From the Eastern Han through the Northern and Southern Dynasties, the finest steel was called hundred-forged fine steel, or hundred-forged steel. Made into knives and swords, it was exceptionally sharp, and was called a precious blade or a precious sword.
In Master Yinguang’s Answering the Questions of a Buddha-Reciting Layman (that is, Zhou Mengyou), he says:
“Q: Do the four lines ‘outside the mind there is no Buddha, outside the Buddha there is no mind’
(these four lines are:
outside the mind there is no Buddha, outside the Buddha there is no mind; the whole mind is the Buddha, the whole Buddha is the mind
refer to nature-virtue? And do the four lines ‘a single thought appearing, a single thought corresponding’
(these four lines are:
a single thought appearing, a single thought corresponding; thought after thought appearing, thought after thought corresponding
refer to cultivation-virtue? A: Both are cultivation-virtue. For ‘outside the mind there is no Buddha, outside the Buddha there is no mind’ is what skill brings about.”
[The two virtues] Nature-virtue and cultivation-virtue. Nature-virtue is the virtue inherent from the start, while cultivation-virtue is the virtue won by practice.
Q: What do the two sets of four lines quoted above mean?
A: These two sets of four lines are very famous; they come from Master Chewu’s Bequeathed Collection
Letter in Reply to Layman Xiangyan. The Master Chewu’s passage is annotated below:

[One must deeply believe and truly understand: outside the mind there is no Buddha, outside the Buddha there is no mind; the whole mind is the Buddha, the whole Buddha is the mind. A single thought appearing is a single thought corresponding; thought after thought appearing is thought after thought corresponding.]

One should deeply believe and truly awaken to this state — “outside the mind there is no Buddha, outside the Buddha there is no mind; the whole mind is the Buddha, the whole Buddha is the mind” — in which only the one thought of reciting the Buddha remains and no other thought exists. When one’s skill reaches this state, then: when a single thought (the pure, undivided thought of reciting the Buddha) appears, a single thought corresponds; when thought after thought appears, thought after thought corresponds.

Here “mind” means the thought of the mind; “Buddha” means the Buddha’s name that is recited; “corresponding” means “this mind becomes the Buddha, this mind is the Buddha.” A single thought corresponding means a single thought’s mind is the Buddha; thought after thought corresponding means thought after thought’s mind is the Buddha.

[Outside the mind there is no Buddha, outside the Buddha there is no mind; the whole mind is the Buddha, the whole Buddha is the mind] Outside the thought of the mind there is no thought of the Buddha (the thought of reciting the Buddha), and outside the thought of the Buddha there is no thought of the mind; the whole thought of the mind is the thought of the Buddha, and the whole thought of the Buddha is the thought of the mind. This describes the state in which the thought of the mind and the thought of the Buddha entirely coincide, and the thought of reciting the Buddha is pure and undefiled.

[Only let this thought constantly appear before you, and that is the true proof. Apart from this thought, to seek proof elsewhere is to be interrupted, to be without intimacy, to enter a forked road! The sutra says, ‘This mind becomes the Buddha, this mind is the Buddha’ — it speaks of precisely this.]

Only let this thought (the pure, undefiled thought of reciting the Buddha) constantly appear before you, and that is the true proof. Apart from this thought, to seek proof elsewhere is to be interrupted, to be without intimacy, to enter a forked road! The sutra says: “This mind becomes the Buddha, this mind is the Buddha.” It speaks of precisely this state!
To recite the Buddha is simply to accomplish this: only let this thought (the pure, undivided thought of reciting the Buddha) constantly appear before you.

In order that “this thought (the pure, undefiled thought of reciting the Buddha) constantly appear before you,” and before one has attained one mind undisturbed, one must first form the good habit of never letting the Buddha’s name be interrupted. This point is supremely important! As it is said, “Before attaining undisturbedness, first make it unbroken.” Master Yinguang says:

“In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in dressing and eating, from morning to night and from night to morning, let not a single phrase of the Buddha’s name be interrupted. Recite it aloud or recite it silently; apart from reciting the Buddha, give rise to no other thought. And if a deluded thought should arise, you must at once make it die away.”
(Letter in Reply to Layman Ye Fubei, I)

In the section “Awareness Turning Without Stop” of Chapter One, “Awareness of Movements,” the Record of Self-Knowledge was used to cultivate the good habit of unbroken awareness; now the Record of Self-Knowledge will be used to cultivate the good habit of an unbroken Buddha’s name.

blocks.text: Chapter Five: Awareness of the Present Thought

inline.s: The moment a delusion arises, be aware; once aware, it is gone.

Awareness of the present thought is also called illuminating awareness of the present thought. When the skill of “awareness of the Buddha’s name” has matured, one may pass on to the cultivation of this stage, “awareness (illuminating awareness) of the present thought”: while reciting the Buddha, be aware of (illuminate) the present thought.

Awareness of the present thought” in Buddha-recitation has two modes: first, intermittent recitation — recite one phrase of the Buddha’s name, then pause a while and closely observe the present thought; second, continuous recitation — recite and observe at once. These two modes may be used flexibly according to the depth of one’s skill and the circumstances.

When one first begins to cultivate awareness of the present thought, one may tire easily; one may intersperse the practices of the earlier stages, or awareness of the Buddha’s name, and then gradually come to be aware of the present thought at all times.

An important exercise: while reciting the Buddha with awareness of the present thought, every phrase of the Buddha’s name must overcome the deluded thoughts. At first, after reciting one phrase, check whether it overcame the deluded thoughts. Once the skill takes hold, you will know while reciting whether it has overcome them. Then, with every phrase you recite, keep clear awareness: has it overcome the deluded thoughts? If not, find the cause and prescribe the right remedy. Persist in this way, and in time, when the skill is proficient, the recitation will naturally become a single continuous piece, neither dull nor scattered. This exercise is very important: if the Buddha’s name can overcome deluded thoughts, it can overcome birth and death. This is a matter of life and death for one’s wisdom-life; you must train at it bitterly.
[Skill becomes a single piece] While reciting the Buddha, no deluded thoughts are mixed in — the thoughts of reciting the Buddha continue into one whole piece.
Master Yinguang says:

“When reciting the Buddha one cannot be pure and undivided; one must control the mind and not let it race outside, and in time it will of itself become pure and undivided. ‘A single piece’ means pure and undefiled.”
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Letter in Reply to Layman Ma Qixi, IV) Master Hanshan says:
“You must clamp your teeth on this one sound of the Buddha
(the Buddha’s name)
and
make it overcome deluded thoughts

. In every place, let thought after thought appear before you, and do not be screened off by deluded thoughts. Working on it bitterly and keenly in this way, in time it becomes pure and proficient, and of itself it corresponds; without seeking a single piece, you become a single piece of yourself.”
(Dream Roaming Collection
Instruction to Layman Jingxin)
On the
One Minute of Chan Concentration

page there is an audio player: after one minute, a bell sounds. (Right-click the play button, and you can set it in the menu to repeat, or download it.) You can use it to measure how long a single phrase of the Buddha’s name can be held without a deluded thought arising. And you can use it as a tool to help you practice gradually lengthening that time. This is basic training of the power of mindfulness, and it is very important; you must train hard and well at it, until a single phrase of the Buddha’s name is invincible wherever it goes.
Q: The patriarchs often speak of letting go. In actual practice it is very difficult; what method should be used to counter it?
A: The Essentials of the Buddhadharma says:
“You should know that when you cannot let go, recite the Buddha with one mind, and you will be able to let go. The Pure Land school’s simile of the pearl that clears muddy water is exactly this.
If the mind races and scatters, oppose it with the Buddha’s name, and in time it will quiet itself.
In learning any Dharma, who does not use bitter effort? If one does not work hard, yet suddenly
jù
, at once)
can let go, why would one need to study at all?”
Master Hanshan says:
“If the mind is deluded, simply recite the Buddha.”
(Dream Roaming Collection · Instruction to Layman Rongyu)
[The simile of the pearl that clears muddy water] Zhongfeng’s Three Periods of Recitation says:

“In the Western Heaven there is a jewel called the clearing pearl. It is said that when this pearl is thrown into muddy water, for every inch it enters, an inch of the muddy water at once becomes clear. As the pearl enters the water, from an inch to a foot, and on to the bottom, the muddy water becomes clear along with it. You should know that the clearing pearl is a figure for the pure thought of reciting the Buddha, and the muddy water a figure for the tangle of deluded mind.”
In the Dream Roaming Collection, Layman Jingxin asked: It is hard for my Buddha-recitation to become a single piece; please instruct me. Master Hanshan taught:

“In practice, the first thing is that the mind seeking liberation from birth and death must be keen. If that mind is not keen, how dare one speak of Buddha-recitation becoming a single piece? Moreover, throughout countless eons sentient beings have had deluded thought after deluded thought, and the roots of their affections are deeply sealed. Even if in this life one leaves the world
(that is, even if in this life one wants to practice and leave the world)
, when has a single thought ever ached for birth and death? In daily use, thought after thought follows the affections
(ordinarily every thought follows the affections and consciousness as they turn)
and one never once turns back to look
(to reflect)
. Now, with a vain and floating faith, you want to cut off the birth and death of many eons — that is what is called saving a pile of firewood with a drop of water; how could such a principle hold
(how could there be any such principle)
? If truly the mind seeking liberation from birth and death were keen, then thought after thought would be as though one’s head were on fire
(burning)
. One only fears that, having lost this human body, a hundred eons would hardly regain it. You must clamp your teeth on this one sound of the Buddha
(the Buddha’s name)
and make it overcome deluded thoughts. In every place, let thought after thought appear before you
(every thought is the thought of the Buddha appearing before you)

, and do not be screened off by deluded thoughts. Working on it bitterly and keenly in this way, in time it becomes pure and proficient, and of itself it corresponds. Then, without seeking a single piece, you become a single piece of yourself. This matter is like a person drinking water, knowing for himself whether it is cold or warm; it cannot be told to another
(there is no way to explain it clearly to another)
, it all depends on your own effort
(it all depends on the person himself realizing it and putting it into practice)
. But if one makes Buddha-recitation merely a face-saving show, then even in the year of the donkey there will be no benefit
(in such a case, even in the year of the donkey there will be no time of benefit — that is, in such a case there will never be any benefit)
. You must simply be brave and fierce, and delay no longer!”
(Dream Roaming Collection · Instruction to Layman Jingxin)
In this instruction, the practice given is:
“You must clamp your teeth on this one sound of the Buddha
(the Buddha’s name)
and make it overcome deluded thoughts. In every place, let thought after thought appear before you
(every thought is the thought of the Buddha appearing before you)

, and do not be screened off by deluded thoughts. Working on it bitterly and keenly in this way, in time it becomes pure and proficient, and of itself it corresponds. Then, without seeking a single piece, you become a single piece of yourself.”

Awareness of the present thought”: in the preliminary stage, the essential point is that it is best to have no deluded thoughts; after that, one must make “the moment a delusion arises, be aware (the moment a deluded thought arises, see it at once)” the essential point of cultivation. Once one has reached this step of “the moment a delusion arises, be aware,” then “once aware, it is gone” is very easy, and by this one reaches the state of not following delusions as they arise, and one mind undisturbed becomes stable.
The moment a delusion arises, be aware

” — this is an important skill in cultivating one mind undisturbed through Buddha-recitation. One must practice it constantly: while reciting the Buddha, watch for the arising of deluded thoughts. In time, one will be able to be aware the moment a delusion arises.

Deluded thoughts arise precisely where awareness is interrupted. To practice “the moment a delusion arises, be aware” is to strengthen the continuity of awareness and close up these interruptions. Therefore the skill of “the moment a delusion arises, be aware” must be done more and more finely and closely.

There are many particular methods for cultivating “the moment a delusion arises, be aware.” For example, recite the Buddha slowly, and after one phrase, observe for a while before reciting the next; or while reciting the Buddha, be aware of your own nature and watch whether deluded thoughts arise; and so on. Practice and experiment more, and you will find many good exercises. Besides training specially on the cushion, supplement it by training off the cushion, at any time and in any place, seizing every spare moment, and your progress will be very fast. With the right method, plus bitter training, success is certain. So for a cultivator who trains hard, the most important thing is to find the practice method that suits him best (recognizing where the path begins).
The old worthies say:
“In cultivation there is no other practice; it lies only in recognizing where the path begins
(that is, in finding the practice method that suits you)
, and once the path’s beginning is recognized
(once you have found the practice method that suits you)
, birth and death come to rest together.”

In fact, to observe closely and study how deluded thoughts arise, and how they then envelop you so that you cannot pull free, is very interesting. More interesting still: the deeper your observation and study go, the less easily deluded thoughts arise, and your skill advances rapidly. For example, you are reciting the Buddha quite well, and the mind is clear and quiet. Suddenly a stream of irritating thoughts arises and will not be waved away. What to do? Quiet your mind and closely observe and study how the deluded thoughts arise, and how they envelop you so that you cannot pull free. Recite one phrase of the Buddha’s name, then observe and study for a while; recite one phrase, then observe and study for a while. This is a wonderful method for getting free of deluded thoughts, and in the very process of getting free, your power grows rapidly. Truly, you should thank these “sparring partners”!

Long ago, a monk went alone into the deep mountains to practice. At night he saw a fierce ghost rush at him. In the crisis he hurriedly recited the Buddha, and the fierce ghost fell back again and again. But the moment the Buddha’s name stopped, the fierce ghost pressed forward again, so he had to recite without cease the whole night through. Only at daybreak did the ghost leave. And so it went for several nights. So the monk
simply

slept by day and recited the Buddha all night long. Year after year the deadlock continued. In the end he attained Buddha-recitation samādhi, and the fierce ghost vanished without a trace. He was exceedingly grateful to that fierce ghost. (Comment: the monk could perfectly well have moved to a place with no fierce ghost, but he advanced into the difficulty. This is the true character of a cultivator.)

In fact, every Buddha-reciter also faces a fierce ghost — deluded thoughts. Day and night it peers at us, wanting to devour our Dharma-body and wisdom-life. So one must keep the highest vigilance and beat back its every attack in good time. The overall outcome is this: either you subdue it and accomplish your own Way, being reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; or it subdues you and leaves you still turning in the six realms.

“Awareness of the present thought” is carried on upon the foundation of the “Preliminary Practices” section and the skill of “awareness of the Buddha’s name.” If you find that something is wrong somewhere, you must make up the lesson in good time and break through the difficulty. This is also a test of our true faith and sincere vows; one must persevere with the tenacity that never turns back a hundred times, and where sincerity reaches, metal and stone are opened. When recitation reaches the point where “the present thought is the thought of the Buddha, and the thought of the Buddha is the present thought,” then one enters one mind undisturbed.
Master Zhongfeng says:

“All you good people! You should know who Amitābha Buddha is: he is the very sentient being who can recite the Buddha. And who are those in the three realms who now follow the two states of suffering and pleasure, and bind up karma for rebirth, toiling day and night without rest? They are the very Buddhas who cannot recite Amitābha.

You should know that this one sound of the Buddha not only cannot be recited in this life; trace it back, and through many eons sunk and stalled in the wheel of suffering, you never once recited it aloud, and so to this day this thought
(the thought of reciting the Buddha)

has not become proficient. Just as you force out two or three recitations, doubt at once arises, tangled worries spring up sideways, vainly troubling the cheeks and tongue to wag, and only sending the spirit racing and scattering. To seek correspondence with the Buddha then is no different from blowing on a net and hoping to fill it.
Why is it so?
(Why does this happen?)
Because
(this is because)
the roots are not deep and the will is unsettled; though one says one is reciting the Buddha, in fact this thought is not together with the Buddha
(that is, while reciting the Buddha the mind and the mouth do not agree)
The ancients’ faith was pure to the utmost, their right cause was awe-inspiring, they took birth and death seriously, and keenly pondered the turning of the wheel
(they truly and keenly reflected on the terror of the six realms of rebirth)
, so ten thousand conditions were laid to rest and cut away
(to lay to rest and cut away: to stop and to cut off)
, a hundred cares melted like ice, and when they raised one sound of the Buddha’s name, at once there was no other seeing
(the thought of the Buddha is the present thought, the present thought is the thought of the Buddha)
Originally,
(a particle introducing the sentence)

the thought that is the Buddha is like the Tai’e sword, laid across the gateway; the Buddha that is the thought is like a great fire-wheel, leaping with stars and blazing flames. It makes all things burn when they touch it and be wounded when they graze it. Recite it long, and outside the thought there is no other Buddha, outside the Buddha no other thought; body and mind are one
(mind and mouth are one)

, and both subject and object are forgotten. Of its words of arrival home, no sound can be permitted; of its talk of a shortcut, why trouble to speak? It may be called the divine art of realizing practice, the true road beyond expedients
(supremely expedient)
, the thunderbolt that shatters the hibernating door of birth and death, the sun and moon that light the dark thoroughfare of delusion.”
(Zhongfeng’s Ritual Manual for the Three Periods of Recitation)

[Outside the thought there is no other Buddha, outside the Buddha no other thought] The present thought is the thought of reciting the Buddha, and the thought of reciting the Buddha is the present thought.

The skill of “awareness of the present thought” is very important; it is the core skill of awareness in Buddha-recitation. It must be practiced over and over on the cushion and off it, with eyes open and eyes closed, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in different surroundings, and before falling asleep. One must make the Buddha’s name overcome deluded thoughts, and not be controlled by them. One must constantly train amid situations and conditions, and test oneself amid situations and conditions. When the skill is deep, it is as Master Zhongfeng says:

“Outside the thought there is no other Buddha, outside the Buddha no other thought; body and mind are one, and both subject and object are forgotten. Of its words of arrival home, no sound can be permitted; of its talk of a shortcut, why trouble to speak? It may be called the divine art of realizing practice, the true road beyond expedients, the thunderbolt that shatters the hibernating door of birth and death, the sun and moon that light the dark thoroughfare of delusion.”
Master Yinguang says:
“It is only that you do not return; return, and you have it — who will dispute the wind and moon of the old home?”
Only then does one begin to understand the wonder of the three words “return, and you have it.”
It is only that you do not return; return, and you have it
] The complete couplet reads:

“You should make the vow, the vow to be reborn — let the traveler’s road of streams and hills be loved by whom it will; it is only that you do not return — return, and you have it: who will dispute the wind and moon of the old home?”
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang · Preface to the Published Collection of Thoughts of Return)
Q: I find awareness of the present thought very difficult. What should I do?

A: Awareness of the present thought is built upon awareness of the Buddha’s name. If you find awareness of the present thought difficult, you may do it in two stages. First, recite the Buddha intermittently: while reciting, be aware of the Buddha’s name, and during the pauses be aware of the present thought. When this stage of skill has matured, pass on naturally to being aware of the present thought at all times. If even the first stage of practice seems beyond you, then you should go on cultivating awareness of the Buddha’s name, and only when the power of awareness has grown strong should you take up awareness of the present thought. The secret of practice is this: it cannot be hurried, it cannot be halted, it must be kept up with constancy, continuous and unbroken. In time, as the skill deepens, you will enter this state: with every phrase of the Buddha’s name you recite, you are clearly aware that from the beginning of this phrase until the beginning of the next, no deluded thought arises in between. This is: “A single thought corresponding, a single thought of the Buddha; thought after thought corresponding, thought after thought of the Buddha.” Further on, it is to consolidate and raise this state, so that habit becomes nature, making it more enduring and more resistant to distraction, until you are “flying in all weathers.”
Q: I recite the Buddha two phrases at a time: two phrases make one set, and five counts make ten phrases; I find this very good at gathering in the mind. May I keep this habit now?

A: Yes. Because you have already formed the habit, you will not be deliberately counting. Now put your attention on reciting each set of the Buddha’s name well; every set must be recited to standard, without deluded thoughts, and then the skill becomes a single piece.
Q: I find “aware the moment a thought arises” too difficult to practice. Is there some expedient?

A: If so, you may borrow Mr. Li Fengshan’s “flat swing exercise” to practice it (for the method of the flat swing exercise, see Chapter One). Because the count for the flat swing exercise is six syllables, when you practice it, silently recite the six-syllable name of the Buddha and put your attention on watching for deluded thoughts to arise. This method is very effective; keep it up, and you will not only be able to “be aware the moment a delusion arises, and once aware it is gone,” but will also be training concentration in movement.
Q: What is contemplating the mind in Buddha-recitation?

A: Contemplating the mind in Buddha-recitation is simply to recite and observe the present thought at once. This chapter, “Awareness of the Present Thought,” is in fact nothing other than contemplating the mind in Buddha-recitation.
A: Not only is there no contradiction; each brings out the best in the other. Master Yinguang says:

“When one first recites the Buddha and has not yet personally realized samādhi, who can be without deluded thoughts? What matters is that the mind always be aware and illuminating, and not follow delusions as they turn.”
(The Essential Record of Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings

Instruction on Methods of Practice) Here “the mind always be aware and illuminating, and not follow delusions as they turn” is precisely contemplating the mind. To recite the Buddha with the skill of contemplating the mind is like a tiger with horns; try it and you will know.
Q: Then why does Master Yinguang say:
“Do not use the method of reciting the Buddha while contemplating the mind; use the method of gathering in the mind to recite the Buddha.”
(Letter in Reply to Layman Yang Weizhang)

A: Because the other party (Layman Yang Weizhang) was a beginner with insufficient foundation, yet adopted contemplation of the mind in Buddha-recitation, and so brought on a rising of the heart-fire; for this reason he wrote to Master Yinguang for instruction. So in this letter Master Yinguang was addressing the other man’s particular situation, giving the medicine to fit the illness, and not denying the practice of contemplating the mind in Buddha-recitation. Master Yinguang wrote: “
You, an ordinary being of extremely heavy karmic power
recklessly use
the method of contemplating the mind,
and so it has come to this
(that is, the ‘rising of the heart-fire’ mentioned in his letter)
.” And he went on: “The method of contemplating the mind is a method of cultivating contemplation in the doctrinal schools; for one who recites the Buddha it is
not very well suited

.” Here “for one who recites the Buddha it is not very well suited” is a euphemism, meaning that your foundation is not yet equal to contemplating the mind in Buddha-recitation, and so the heart-fire rose. Therefore
Master Yinguang told him:
“Do not use the method of reciting the Buddha while contemplating the mind; use the method of gathering in the mind to recite the Buddha.”

Contemplating the mind in Buddha-recitation is wonderful, but it does not suit those whose foundation is insufficient. Because beginners lack sufficient foundation, if they contemplate the mind in Buddha-recitation they often experience dizziness, headache, and rising of the heart-fire. That is why this book (Awareness in Buddha-Recitation), in treating “awareness of the present thought (contemplating the mind in Buddha-recitation),” has already laid a solid foundation through the Preliminary Practices (awareness of movements, awareness of sensations, awareness of breathing, awareness of the present moment, awareness of thoughts) and through “awareness of the Buddha’s name.” In his Essay on Groping for the Elephant in Buddha-Recitation Samādhi, Master Yinguang instructs:
“As for the method, ”
one must

when reciting the Buddha, turn the recitation back to observe, focusing on one state and not letting the mind race outward, so that thought after thought tends the source of the mind, and mind after mind accords with the Buddha-substance.”
Is that not contemplating the mind in Buddha-recitation? Therefore one who would recite the Buddha by the method of contemplating the mind must first possess a certain foundation.
Contemplating the mind in Buddha-recitation is the very essence of reciting the Buddha’s name; since ancient times many patriarchs and great masters have attained one mind undisturbed through it.
Q: When I contemplate the mind in Buddha-recitation, I feel dizzy. What should I do?

A: This is because the power of awareness is not strong enough. You should first work hard at the Preliminary Practices to strengthen your awareness; when awareness is strong enough, then contemplate the mind in Buddha-recitation, and you will not feel dizzy.
Q: When contemplating the mind, where should the contemplation be started?

A: On this point, Mr. Nan Huaijin says: “The pure method of prajñā contemplation of mind observes the arising and ceasing of one’s own mind-consciousness; there is originally no question of where contemplation should start — that is fussing like an old woman, a needless complication! The mind is not in the inside, the outside, or in between. Yet when ordinary practitioners do this contemplation, they easily concentrate attention in the head, causing high blood pressure and other ailments; and so a further expedient was offered, to contemplate lightly at the heart. And lest you not understand what is meant by the heart, it was specially explained as the pit of the stomach, between the two nipples, at the hollow where the ribs meet. Contemplate naturally right there.” (A First Course in Concentration and Insight)
[Between the two nipples] The midpoint of the line between the two nipples, commonly called the yellow court, the heart-wheel, or the heart’s head; it is also the location of the Shanzhong point.
To show how important contemplating the mind is for a student of the Buddha, the following instruction is quoted specially:
The old worthies say:
“If one does not contemplate the mind, the Dharma has no place to come from.”

Because the Buddhadharma is all on the pure mind; only by turning the light inward and illuminating within can the Buddha-nature be drawn forth, and then all gates of samādhi, all gates of dhāraṇī, all gates of liberation, and all gates of spiritual power appear at once. So you should know that the mind is where the wondrous Dharma comes from; if one does not contemplate the mind, how can it be drawn out? Therefore contemplating the mind is the foremost wondrous practice of the Buddhadharma, and no other practice can equal it.
[The gate of dhāraṇī] The Sanskrit dhāraṇī
is translated into Chinese as:
“total retention.”
Because

the bodhisattva, by the Dharma of total retention, follows the speech and sounds of all sentient beings, opens and guides them to right faith, causes them to extinguish all unwholesome minds and practice all wholesome dharmas: this is the bodhisattva’s gate of dhāraṇī.
The Sutra of the Mahāyāna Contemplation of the Mind Ground says:

“In the three realms the mind is sovereign; one who can contemplate the mind attains ultimate liberation, while one who cannot remains forever in bondage.” “This Dharma is called the supreme secret mind-ground Dharma-gate of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions; this Dharma is called the sudden-enlightenment Dharma-gate by which all ordinary beings enter the Tathāgata’s ground; this Dharma is called the true right road by which all bodhisattvas go toward great bodhi; this Dharma is called the subtle jewel-palace in which the Buddhas of the three times enjoy the Dharma-bliss of their own; this Dharma is called the inexhaustible treasury that benefits all sentient beings.”
The Nirvāṇa Sutra says:
“To be able to contemplate the mind-nature is called supreme concentration.”
Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch of Chan, says:

“A hundred thousand Dharma-gates all return to the square inch; virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all in the source of the mind. All gates of precepts, of concentration, of wisdom, and all spiritual transformations are complete in themselves, not apart from your mind.”
The Fifth Patriarch Hongren says:
“If one does not know one’s original mind, learning the Dharma brings no benefit.”
The Sixth Patriarch Huineng says:

“Good friends! Without awakening, the Buddha is a sentient being; at the moment of a single thought of awakening, the sentient being is the Buddha. So you should know that all dharmas are wholly within your own mind — why not, from within the mind, suddenly see the true suchness of your own nature? The Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra says: ‘My original self-nature is from the first pure; if one knows one’s own mind and sees the nature, all attain the Buddha Way.’ The Vimalakīrti Sutra says: ‘At that very moment, suddenly opened, one regains the original mind.’ Good friends! In Master Ren’s place, at a single word I awakened on the spot and suddenly saw the true suchness of my own nature. Therefore I spread this teaching abroad, so that students of the Way may suddenly awaken to bodhi. Each of you, contemplate your own mind and see your own nature.”
Therefore the root of the Buddhadharma is the mind, and the root of practice is contemplation.
To contemplate and illuminate constantly is for prajñā to permeate ignorance.
Once ignorance is broken, the Dharma-body appears at once. Leaping straight into the Tathāgata’s ground, without passing through eons one obtains the Dharma-body.
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“All Tathāgatas, from the causal ground of their original arising, rely on perfect illumination of the pure enlightened mark, forever cutting off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha Way.”
Bodhidharma’s Treatise on Breaking the Marks says:
“Question: If there is a person who aspires to the Buddha Way, what Dharma should he practice to be most economical? Answer:
Only the one Dharma of contemplating the mind encompasses all dharmas; it is the most economical.

Question: How can one Dharma encompass all dharmas? Answer: The mind is the root of all dharmas; all dharmas are born only from the mind. If one understands the mind, all dharmas are complete — like a great tree, whose branches, flowers, and fruit all depend on the root. He who plants a tree keeps the root and only then gets fruit; he who fells a tree removes the root and it must die. If one understands the mind and cultivates the Way, little effort brings easy success; if one does not understand the mind and cultivates, effort is wasted and brings no benefit. So you should know that all good and evil come from one’s own mind. To seek elsewhere, outside the mind, is in the end to be nowhere.”
On the supreme importance of contemplating the mind, Master Yinguang, recounting how Śākyamuni Buddha attained the Way, writes:
“At the age of nineteen

, in the middle of the night of the eighth day of the second month, he mounted the horse Kanthaka, crossed the city wall, and went straight to the deep mountains to practice the Way beyond the world. And wishing to show that the paths of the outsiders were not the right Dharma, he wandered for five more years, visiting all the immortals. Afterward he
sat alone contemplating the mind

, eating one sesame seed and one grain of wheat a day, practicing austerities for six years; and on the eighth day of the twelfth month, when the morning star appeared, he raised his eyes and looked — and was suddenly greatly enlightened. He sighed: ‘How wonderful, how wonderful! All sentient beings possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue-marks. But because of deluded thinking and attachment, they cannot realize them. If they were free of deluded thinking, then all-wisdom, natural wisdom, and unobstructed wisdom would at once appear.’”
(A Talk to the Chaoyang Buddhist Association, I)
The moon reaches the high peak, and all things are pure; the mind holds the Buddha’s name, and ten thousand conditions are empty.
To sum up the above, the cultivation of awareness in Buddha-recitation has three stages:
Stage one: awareness of the Buddha’s name — while reciting the Buddha, be aware of the thought of reciting, knowing as you recite, the mind not wandering aside.

Stage two: awareness of the present thought — while reciting the Buddha, be aware of the present thought; when a deluded thought arises you can see it, can turn it away with the Buddha’s name, and do not follow it as it arises.

Stage three: no other thought — while reciting the Buddha, the thought of reciting is the present thought, and the present thought is the thought of reciting; mind and Buddha are one, and one mind undisturbed is attained.

Keep practicing by the methods introduced above. Then one day you will suddenly find that, while reciting the Buddha, you are spontaneously and clearly aware of the present thought; and at that moment, apart from remembering and reciting the Buddha, there is no other thought — quietly, purely, you are remembering and reciting the Buddha. This is one mind undisturbed, also called unconfused mindfulness.
As Master Yinguang says in his Essay on Groping for the Elephant in Buddha-Recitation Samādhi:

“When the Buddha’s name is raised, deluded thoughts vanish utterly; a coolness permeates the body, and joy fills the breast. It is exactly like sweet dew poured over the crown, like ghee irrigating the heart; its bliss cannot be described.”

When the thought of reciting the Buddha is pure and undefiled, that is the state in which mind and Buddha are one — a single thought corresponding, a single thought of the Buddha; thought after thought corresponding, thought after thought of the Buddha; this mind becomes the Buddha, this mind is the Buddha. Only let this thought constantly appear before you, and that is the true proof.

The next step is to consolidate and deepen this state of one mind undisturbed, making it enduring and resistant to distraction, so that under any circumstances you can raise the Buddha’s name, smoothly enter one mind undisturbed, and abide in it continuously — accumulated habit becoming nature. For this you must, at all times and in all places, use the Buddha’s name as the anchoring needle of the sea and do the work of the three minds (gathering in the mind, guarding the mind, and steadying the mind). When the work of the three minds is proficient, the Buddha’s name of one mind undisturbed can continue unbroken from a hundred to a thousand, from a thousand to ten thousand — thought succeeding thought. Master Shandao says:
“Sentient beings have heavy obstacles, the states are subtle and the mind coarse, the consciousness flurries and the spirit flies, so contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore the Great Sage
(that is, Śākyamuni Buddha)

in compassion urged them simply to recite the Name exclusively. Precisely because reciting the Name is easy, one is reborn by continuing it. If one can continue thought after thought, making this life the term, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn. ... I hope all people will consider this well: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, one must rouse the mind and master oneself, never neglecting it day or night; when the former thought ends at death, the latter thought is at once reborn, forever enjoying the bliss of the unconditioned Dharma, until Buddhahood itself — is that not joy!”
(For details see
The Pure Land Teaching of Master Shandao

[Gathering in the mind, guarding the mind, and steadying the mind] Gathering in the mind is to draw back the mind that has already been lost. Guarding the mind is to hold firmly the mind once drawn back. Steadying the mind is, at the moment when the mind is about to be lost but is not yet lost, to steady it and make it immovable — like reining in a horse at the edge of a cliff.
Master Xingce (the Tenth Patriarch of the Pure Land school) says:
“In the seven days
(the seven days of an intensive Buddha-recitation retreat)

of reciting the Name, what matters is one mind undisturbed, without interval and without mixture; it is not necessarily fast recitation or much recitation that wins. Only recite the Name closely, neither slow nor hurried, so that the Buddha’s name in the mind is perfectly clear; in dressing and eating, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, let one phrase of the great Name be continuous and close-packed, like breathing itself, neither scattered nor sunk. Reciting the Name thus, one may be called one who can be single-minded and diligent in practice.”
(Pure Land Warnings
Instruction to the Assembly at the Beginning of the Intensive Seven-Day Period)
Master Pudu says:

“Whoever cultivates the Pure Land must be utterly resolved to do battle with birth and death; it is not a matter of speaking and then resting. You should reflect that impermanence is swift and time waits for no one, and that you must take this as the one thing to be done. If you can believe it, then from today rouse great, brave, and diligent effort; do not ask whether you understand or not, whether you see the nature or not — simply hold fast to one phrase, Namo Amitābha Buddha, as though leaning on a Mount Sumeru, unshakable. Make your mind single, your intent undivided; whether by contemplating, reciting, remembering, or the ten recitations, whether silently, exclusively, continuously, or reverently — recite, and here, and always remember, always recite. Recite in the morning, recite in the evening, recite walking, recite sitting; let no thought of the mind pass in vain, let recitation of the Buddha never leave the mind; day after day, hour after hour, never let it go. Dense and close, like a hen brooding on eggs, always keeping the warmth unbroken — that is pure thought in succession. Add to this the illumination of wisdom, and you know that the Pure Land is your own mind: this is the practice of one of superior wisdom. If you can hold fast thus, take charge thus, and lean thus, then even when states of suffering and pleasure, favor and adversity appear, you simply recite Amitābha Buddha, without a single thought of change, of retreat, or of distraction, until the end of life, forever without another thought — you will certainly be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. If you can truly practice in this way, then the ignorance of many eons and the karmic obstacles of birth and death will of themselves dissolve, and the dust of affliction and the outflows of habit will of themselves be cleansed; you will see Amitābha face to face, never apart from your own thought; when the work is done and the practice complete, vow-power and practice aiding each other, at the end of life you will certainly be reborn in the highest grade.”
(The Precious Mirror of the Pure Land School)
[Vow-power and practice aiding each other] Faith and vows, and earnest practice, rely on and support each other.

When the skill has reached this point, it is like a poor man who has found treasure: he must learn to use this wish-fulfilling pearl well, and not go on living in cold and hunger. Since one already has the ability to recite the Buddha with one mind undisturbed, one can and should turn karma with the mind and dissolve karma with the mind, until karma is dissolved and wisdom shines, obstacles are exhausted and blessings abound, and whatever one does prospers, swiftly ascending to the highest grade. For the particular method, see
Turning Karma with the Mind
Q: Master Shandao says:

“Precisely because reciting the Name is easy, one is reborn by continuing it. If one can continue thought after thought, making this life the term, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.”
What expedient is there for continuing thought after thought?

A: You may use the method of stringing beads on a golden thread: when one phrase of the Buddha’s name has been recited and the thought of reciting still has more to give, hold it a while until the next phrase begins, so that two neighboring phrases of the Buddha’s name are threaded together by the intent, with no deluded thought between. Continue reciting in this way, and you will of yourself continue thought after thought. As the power of mindfulness grows, the interval between two phrases may gradually be lengthened while the intent remains unbroken. In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, always take good care of the practice and do not let it be lost; let the Buddha-thought alone appear before you, uninterrupted and unbroken, until it is trained to perfect purity, fused into one whole. The Three Periods of Recitation of Zhongfeng says:

“Raise one sound of the Buddha’s name, and at once there is no other seeing. It is like the Tai’e sword laid across the gateway; like a great fire-wheel, leaping with stars and blazing flames. All things burn when they touch it and are wounded when they graze it. Straight on to one mind undisturbed, where both subject and object are forgotten. Of its words of arrival home, no further mention can be made; of its talk of a shortcut, why trouble to speak? It may be called: the divine art of realizing practice, the true road beyond expedients; the thunderbolt that shatters the hibernating door of birth and death, the sun and moon that light the dark thoroughfare of delusion.”
[The power of mindfulness] The power of exclusive mindfulness, able to withstand distraction and temptation. In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching, the Buddha says:
“If the power of mindfulness is firm and strong, then even among the thieves of the five desires one is not harmed.”

[The five desires] The cravings for form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form means beautiful appearances; sound means pleasing sounds and attractive speech; smell means fragrant scents; taste means delicious flavors; touch means agreeable sensations of contact. Because these five can give rise to greed in people, they are called the five desires. To keep the precepts pure is to be able to control the five faculties and not be moved by the five desires.
In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching, the Buddha says:

“You monks, having been able to abide in the precepts, should control the five faculties and not let them run loose into the five desires. It is like a cowherd who takes up his staff and watches them, not letting them wander and trample the young crops.”
[The five faculties] Eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Seize every spare moment; accumulated habit becomes nature.

To sum up, the skill of one mind undisturbed has four levels: one, ten phrases undisturbed; two, a hundred phrases undisturbed; three, a thousand phrases undisturbed; four, undisturbed at all times. What is usually called one mind undisturbed means undisturbed at all times. This is the goal every Buddha-reciter should reach, and the goal every Buddha-reciter can reach; hence it is said: ten thousand practice and ten thousand arrive.

In terms of time, ten phrases of the Buddha’s name take about nine seconds, a hundred phrases about a minute and a half, a thousand phrases about fifteen minutes. Of course this is only a reference figure, since each person’s pace of recitation differs; you can measure your own.
Master Jieliu (the Tenth Patriarch of the Pure Land school) instructed at an intensive Buddha-recitation retreat:
“In the seven days of reciting the Name, what matters is one mind undisturbed, without interval and without mixture; it is not necessarily fast recitation or much recitation that wins.”
(Pure Land Warnings) So in reciting the Buddha, what is best is what gathers in the mind and endures.
The general method for cultivating one mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation is:
recite and observe at once
(the present thought)
— reciting the Buddha while contemplating the mind, contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha.

Reciting in this way, if the power of awareness is focused and continuous, deluded thoughts do not arise; and even if there is an occasional lapse and a deluded thought arises, you can be aware of it at once. Moreover, as you recite the Buddha, the power of awareness is constantly growing stronger — and this is the most crucial point of all. When the power of awareness has grown strong enough, deluded thoughts will of themselves vanish, and you will clearly “see” that in the mind there is only the Buddha’s name and no other thought. Someone asked Elder Master Guangqin for the secret of reciting the Buddha, and he answered:
“There is no secret at all; just watch your own mind.”

(The Fruit Master Who Is at Ease Everywhere) Remember: at all times and in all places, “just watch your own mind”! If a deluded thought arises, know it and do not follow it; do not be disturbed by it.

[There is no secret at all; just watch your own mind] There is no other secret: when reciting the Buddha, you must simply watch your own thoughts. [Know it and do not follow it] Watch this deluded thought without judging it. The key to “know it and do not follow it” is to work on the “knowing”: watch as a cat watches a mouse hole, so that the moment a thought arises you know it. Once you can “know it the moment it arises,” “not following it” becomes easy.

To reach these four levels, you must in the course of practice constantly find problems, solve problems, and advance step by step. The method is: practice, ponder, sum up, improve; then practice again, ponder again, sum up again, improve again;
. Continue in this way, and you will find the good method that suits you best.

To recite ten phrases of the Buddha’s name well is the foundation of foundations, so you must first work bitterly at ten phrases undisturbed. The skill of ten phrases undisturbed is built on the method of the ten recitations counted.
Because this method has already become proficient, you need not deliberately count while reciting the Buddha, but simply observe the present thought.

The ten phrases of the Buddha’s name must be recited as one fused whole, with no gap to enter. No sooner is the Buddha’s name raised than the ten phrases come out in file by instinct, and you clearly “see” that in the mind there is only the Buddha’s name and no other thought.

These ten phrases of the Buddha’s name must be well trained; train by seizing every spare moment, recite by seizing every spare moment, and make it endure without slackening. When a deluded thought arises, that is karma binding the mind; to replace the deluded thought with the Buddha’s name is the mind turning karma. You must at all times and in all places replace deluded thoughts with the Buddha’s name: if ten phrases will not do, then ten more, and so continue, constantly turning karma with the mind, and in time, as the skill deepens, the wonder of it cannot be described. The Caigentan says:

“Where a thought arises, as soon as you feel it heading down the road of desire, pull it back onto the road of principle. To be aware the moment it arises, and to turn it the moment you are aware — this is the juncture at which disaster is turned to blessing, at which the dead come back to life; never let it pass lightly.”
On the method of the ten recitations counted, Master Yinguang instructs:

“The so-called ten recitations counted means that when reciting the Buddha, from one phrase to ten phrases, you must recite them clearly and also remember them clearly. Having reached ten phrases, you must again recite from one phrase to ten, and not go on to twenty or thirty. Count as you recite, and do not use a bead-counter; rely on the mind alone to remember. If it is hard to remember ten phrases straight through, then divide them into two breaths: from one to five, and from six to ten
(two sets of five phrases)
. If that too is tiring, then recite from one to three, from four to six, and from seven to ten, in three breaths
(three, three, four)
. Recite clearly, remember clearly, hear clearly, and deluded thoughts have nowhere to set foot; one mind undisturbed will in time be attained of itself.

You should know that these ten recitations and the morning ten recitations are the same in gathering in deluded thoughts but very different in the effort used. In the morning ten recitations, one full breath makes one recitation, regardless of how many phrases of the Buddha are said. Here one phrase of the Buddha makes one recitation. The former can be done only in the morning ten recitations; if done twenty or thirty times, it injures the breath and causes illness. Here, reciting one phrase of the Buddha, the mind knows one phrase; reciting ten phrases of the Buddha, the mind knows ten phrases. From one to ten, from one to ten, even if one recites tens of thousands of phrases a day, all are counted in this way. It not only removes deluded thoughts but is also most nourishing to the spirit. Fast or slow, there is no obstruction at all. From morning to night, it is suitable at all times. Compared with those who count with beads, its benefit is worlds apart. That way the body toils and the spirit is stirred; this way the body is at ease and the mind at peace.

But when one is doing work, counting may be difficult; then recite earnestly and simply. When the work is done, again gather in the mind and count. Then the thoughts that come and go in crowds will all follow along into the Buddha’s name focused on one state. Mahāsthāmaprāpta said, ‘Gathering in the six sense faculties, pure thoughts in succession, one attains samādhi; this is foremost.’ For those of keen faculties there is no need to speak of it. But for dull roots like ours, if we set aside this method of the ten recitations counted and want to gather in the six sense faculties and continue pure thoughts in succession, it is very hard! Very hard

Again, you should know that this method of gathering in the mind to recite the Buddha is a wonder inconceivable, at once shallow and deep, at once small and great. Simply believe the Buddha’s words with reverence, and do not, because your own view cannot reach so far, give rise to doubt, and so lose the roots of goodness of many eons and fail to obtain the ultimate true benefit — that would be pitiable.

Counting beads while reciting the Buddha is suitable only when walking or standing. If one sits quietly to nourish the spirit, the movement of the hand keeps the spirit from settling, and in time one falls ill. This method of the ten recitations counted is suitable in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down alike. When lying down, one should only recite silently, not aloud. If aloud, first it is disrespectful, and second it injures the breath. Remember this! Remember this!”
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang · Letter in Reply to Layman Gao Shaolin, IV)

[Then the thoughts that come and go in crowds will all follow along into the Buddha’s name focused on one state] “Cong cong” (chōng chōng) means the appearance of coming and going without cease. Here “those who come and go in crowds” means the thoughts that come and go without cease. “Following along” means that like follows like. The meaning of the whole sentence is: because one gathers in the mind and counts, the thoughts that come and go without cease also become, one after another, the Buddha’s name focused on one state.
